questions.explain: Switching to FULL is not retroactive — you need a full backup after the switch to start the log chain, otherwise log backup attempts will fail and your RPO is silently unprotected.
options: Nothing — the switch immediately starts the log chain from the last SIMPLE checkpoint.
You must take a full backup after the switch; until that base exists, log backups cannot form a valid chain.
You must run DBCC CHECKDB once to reset the recovery model.
You must cycle the SQL Server error log with sp_cycle_errorlog.
questions.q: You switch a database from SIMPLE to FULL recovery model so you can take log backups. What must happen before a valid log backup chain exists?

questions.explain: NORECOVERY leaves the database in restoring mode so subsequent backups can be applied; using RECOVERY on an intermediate step brings the database online and blocks further restores.
options: NORECOVERY compresses the backup files so they fit on disk.
NORECOVERY is required only when the database is in BULK_LOGGED recovery model.
NORECOVERY prevents CHECKSUM validation errors during intermediate restores.
NORECOVERY keeps the database in restoring mode so subsequent backups can be applied; using RECOVERY on an intermediate step brings the database online and blocks further restores.
questions.q: In a point-in-time restore sequence (full → differential → log backups), why must every restore except the final one use WITH NORECOVERY?

questions.explain: A tail-log backup captures the tail of the log — transactions after the last scheduled log backup — so including it as the final step in the restore sequence can shrink the data-loss window to zero.
options: It verifies the integrity of the full backup without restoring it.
It captures transactions committed after the last scheduled log backup, potentially reducing data loss to zero.
It shrinks the transaction log so the restore completes faster.
It converts a differential backup into a full backup.
questions.q: What does a tail-log backup (BACKUP LOG ... WITH NO_TRUNCATE, NORECOVERY) give you during disaster recovery?

questions.explain: BULK_LOGGED minimally logs bulk operations, so they don't bloat the log, but you cannot stop at a moment inside the bulk window during a restore — only at the end of the log backup that contains the bulk-logged changes.
options: You lose point-in-time recovery across the bulk window — you can only restore to the end of a log backup containing bulk-logged changes, not to a moment inside it.
Point-in-time recovery works exactly as in FULL recovery model.
BULK_LOGGED automatically switches to SIMPLE after each bulk operation.
Log backups are not possible at all in BULK_LOGGED.
questions.q: A database in BULK_LOGGED recovery model runs BULK INSERT nightly. What is the consequence for point-in-time recovery?

questions.explain: Log shipping uses Agent jobs to take, copy, and restore log backups (with STANDBY or NORECOVERY). There is no automatic failover; on disaster you manually bring the standby online, and RPO equals the shipping interval (typically ~15 minutes).
options: It provides automatic failover coordinated by WSFC, just like an Availability Group.
It is a scheduled copy-and-restore of transaction-log backups with no automatic failover; RPO equals the shipping interval and failover is manual with RESTORE ... WITH RECOVERY.
It requires shared storage between the primary and standby servers.
It only works when both servers are in the same Windows domain.
questions.q: Which statement about SQL Server log shipping is TRUE?
